transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-11
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood SE), Dana (PeregrineAI Head of Product), Owen (PeregrineAI ML Eng), Lina (CTO), Marcus (Security)

Summary: Brief walkthrough of Redwood's Eval/Quality monitoring features (Prompt Sets, Regression Alerts, A/B comparisons and traffic splits). Discussed POC scope, data flow for prompt-level monitoring, security concerns (VPC/private), and next steps for pilot.

Topics: 1) Prompt set instrumentation and labeling 2) Automated regression alerts and thresholds 3) A/B compare + traffic split setup 4) Integration touchpoints (API vs Console) 5) Security/compliance considerations

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — uh — appreciate you making time. We're Jordan from Redwood, AE. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Dana: Hi Jordan, Dana here. Thanks.
[00:10] Owen: Owen.
[00:11] Lina: Lina — hi.
[00:13] Marcus: Marcus from security.
[00:15] Sofia: Sofia here, SE. I'll be walking through the product after a quick kickoff.
[00:20] Jordan: Cool. Our goal today is to demo how you can instrument prompt sets, set up regression alerts, and run A/B comparisons with traffic splits. We'll leave time for infra/security questions near the end.
[00:31] Owen: Quick context — we're running a hybrid setup. Most of our inference is on dedicated GPUs in GCP right now, but we have a compliance track that might want private VPC. We also need to show improvement over our current baseline for coherency and hallucination rates.
[00:44] Jordan: Perfect. That lines up with what Sofia will demo: Console for quick visualization, API for programmatic eval ingestion, and Optimize recommendations for batching/quant.
[00:55] Sofia: Okay pulling up the console — excuse me if the clip is a little slow on my end. So this is the EvalOps module, we call it "Prompt Health" here — I know sometimes the transcriber calls it Prompt Hub or uh, Prompt Guard, so names can vary —
[01:12] Speaker 1: (laughs)
[01:13] Sofia: On the left is your prompt sets view. You can create sets from S3, paste csv, or connect via API. For PeregrineAI we'd recommend three starter sets: "Customer-Facing Answers", "Internal Summaries", and "Code-synthesis cases". Each set carries expected labels and primary metrics — coherence, factuality, and response length distribution.
[01:34] Dana: How do you instrument a prompt to map to our internal categories? We have several production prompts that morph a bit based on user intent.
[01:40] Sofia: Great question. You can attach tags at ingestion time. If you send via the Redwood eval ingestion API there are optional fields: prompt_id, intent_tag, scenario. Or via the console you can bulk-apply mappings. For dynamic prompts we recommend using a canonical key — e.g., prompt_template_id — and then pass variable substitution at runtime. That way evals map to the set even if the exact text changes.
[02:04] Owen: If we do that programmatically, what's the latency impact? We're sensitive to token p99.
[02:10] Sofia: The instrumentation is asynchronous — sending telemetry to the Eval pipeline doesn't add to generation latency. Only when you call the eval API synchronously for a golden reference will it affect latency, but most customers run batched eval ingestion. Our Optimize module suggests batching thresholds based on your seq-length distribution to keep cost down.
[02:29] Owen: Okay makes sense. Can you show the A/B compare flow?
[02:32] Sofia: Sure — switching to the A/B workspace. Here you can create an experiment, specify variants (model v1, model v2 / quantized variant), and configure traffic splits. You can target by route, percent traffic, or by user cohort via the SDK.
[02:48] Sofia: For example, we set 70/30 traffic split to test a multi-quantized variant. The dashboard will show side-by-side metrics — lift/loss on coherence, flagged hallucinations, token cost, and latency. You can also run pairwise comparisons with statistical significance bounds.
[03:04] Dana: We need to show exec-level impact: cost delta vs quality delta. Does Redwood provide an exportable report?
[03:10] Sofia: Yes, you can export a one-page report and a CSV of per-prompt metrics. We also surface token-level cost estimates and per-route latency percentiles so you can present that to finance.
[03:20] Owen: On regression alerts — can they be tied to specific prompt sets and thresholded?
[03:24] Sofia: Absolutely. Alerts can be scoped to prompt sets, to tag filters, or to routes. You set either absolute thresholds or relative drift from baseline. For instance, alert if hallucination rate increases by 3 percentage points or if median coherence drops below 0.75. Alerts support escalation: email, Slack, webhook, PagerDuty.
[03:42] Marcus: From security: what data leaves our VPC? We can't send customer PII to third-party storage.
[03:49] Jordan: Good point. For the POC we can run Redwood Private — that'll keep inference and telemetry in your VPC and we can either route telemetry to your internal S3-compatible store or enable on-prem archive. We also support encrypted in-transit and at-rest keys via KMS/HSM integration.
[04:07] Marcus: Do you have an SOC 2 report and can we do an on-site audit?
[04:11] Jordan: We have SOC 2 Type II. I will send the security pack after the call. For deeper audits we can coordinate via our security team; we'll note that as a next step.
[04:21] Lina: On the POC scope — we typically need to run a 4-week pilot with baseline evaluation and a live A/B test. We want to measure hallucination, throughput, and unit cost. Can Redwood's metrics integrate with our existing observability stack?
[04:33] Sofia: Yes. We emit metrics to Prometheus/Grafana and have a direct CloudWatch export for AWS customers. For GCP you can export to Stackdriver / Cloud Monitoring. You can also pull raw per-request traces via our tracing hooks to link with your APM.
[04:48] Owen: A technical nit — how do you compute hallucination automatically? We don't have a perfect oracle for every prompt.
[04:53] Sofia: Right — our approach is hybrid. You can plug in automated classifiers (we provide an ensemble) to flag likely hallucinations, then stitch in human labels for a subset. Over time a small human-in-the-loop training set greatly improves automated detection. We show confidence intervals and support manual overrides per prompt set.
[05:12] Jordan: One thing we often recommend is a stratified sampling plan so you don't over-index on rare failure cases. For POC we'll help design that sampling.
[05:19] Dana: Okay, demo time?
[05:21] Sofia: Yep. I'll step through creating an experiment. First I create prompt set from csv — uploaded a small sample we pre-populated for Peregrine. (screen share) You can see each row has prompt_template_id, user_intent, expected_label.
[05:34] Speaker 1: there's a bit of echo on Dana's mic
[05:36] Sofia: Now I configure metrics — coherence (0-1), factuality score (classifier), avg tokens, and a custom business metric "satisfaction" which can be fed from post-call surveys.
[05:48] Sofia: Creating experiment — variants: baseline model (gpt-ish-open-3) and quant-optimized variant (gpt-open-3-q4). I set 60/40 split for a limited cohort. Hit start.
[06:02] Sofia: As data streams in you'll see the compare UI populate. This sample has only a few dozen responses so confidence intervals are wide — we show that as gray bands.
[06:12] Owen: That UI — can we link back to the raw prompts and output to review examples?
[06:16] Sofia: Yep, you can drill into a metric, click "view examples", and it shows per-prompt outputs side-by-side with the model outputs, classifier flags, and human annotations where available.
[06:28] Dana: Nice. On the side you mentioned Optimize recommendations — what does that look like?
[06:33] Sofia: Optimize analyzes your request distribution and suggests batching targets, quantization profiles, and candidate fallback models. For example, if you have many short prompts it may recommend smaller batch sizes to keep latency low; for long generations it finds sweet spots for continuous batching. It also flags where quantized variants might be acceptable based on metric lift.
[06:50] Lina: Any built-in change detection to avoid noisy alerts when you roll new code? We deploy frequently.
[06:55] Sofia: Yes — you can link alerts to deploy metadata (git sha, release tag). We support suppressions during known deploy windows and have a cooldown period option so transient spikes don't fire an alert.
[07:08] Owen: On the API side, how do we send evaluation results? Is there a single endpoint?
[07:12] Sofia: There's a bulk ingestion endpoint and a realtime endpoint. Bulk is recommended for periodic uploads (CSV or newline json). Realtime is rpc-style for synchronous golden evaluations. Both accept attributes for prompt_set, prompt_id, labels, and metadata. We also provide SDKs in Python and Node.
[07:28] Marcus: Encryption: can we enforce customer-managed keys?
[07:31] Jordan: Yep — CMKs via KMS/HSM supported in Private deployments. For hosted we also support envelope encryption with customer-provided keys in some enterprise contracts.
[07:41] Dana: Cost question — what's the expected extra cost for running EvalOps during the pilot? We don't want eval plumbing to double our bill.
[07:49] Jordan: Eval ingestion itself is modest — mostly storage and classifier compute. We publish token-level cost estimates in the report. For a typical pilot size (100k evals over 4 weeks) customers see low single-digit percent overhead compared to inference spend; we'll provide a tailored estimate once we see your sample.
[08:05] Owen: If we run the A/B split and want automatic rollback if quality drops, is that supported?
[08:10] Sofia: Yes — we have automatic fallback policies. You can define a guardrail: if rolling metric breaches threshold for X minutes, traffic automatically shifts back to a safe variant and an alert is fired. This is used a lot in Dedicated setups.
[08:24] Lina: For the POC, do we need to provision dedicated capacity?
[08:27] Jordan: Not initially — we can run the pilot on hosted endpoints with a private VPC link for telemetry, or set up a temporary dedicated pool if you want to validate scale. Given your compliance needs, Private deployment might be the long-term plan but pilot can start hosted with strict network controls.
[08:43] Dana: Great. A few follow-ups from our side: we'll send example prompt sets and our current baseline metrics. Also Marcus will follow-up with specific encryption questions.
[08:52] Jordan: Awesome. We'll also send the security pack and an example POC plan. Sofia, Evan — anything to add?
[08:59] Evan: I'll put together a sample notebook for running pairwise significance tests using our exported CSVs — share that in the repo.
[09:07] Sofia: And I'll share the quickstart deck and a short checklist for prompt instrumentation.
[09:12] Dana: Cool — timeline expectations? If we get the sample data in next week, can we start the POC 4/20?
[09:18] Jordan: That looks doable. We'll tentatively pencil in 2027-04-20 for kickoff and confirm after we review the samples.
[09:25] Speaker 2: (background) thanks everyone
[09:27] Jordan: Okay closing recap: Jordan will send pricing + security pack, Sofia send deck + notebook links, Evan send pairwise test notebook, PeregrineAI to send prompt sets and baseline metrics. We'll target POC kickoff 2027-04-20.
[09:42] Dana: Thanks all.
[09:44] Owen: Thanks.
[09:45] Lina: Thanks.
[09:46] Marcus: bye

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and minor transcription errors expected (e.g., product strings like "EvalOps" transcribed as "eval ups" or "prompt hub").
